en: (7) The seventh chapter, the Miscellaneous Section, which is a treasury of jewels of well-spoken verses.

The text here is excerpted from the seventh book of the *Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra*, edited by Nārāyaṇa Rāma Ācārya Kāvyatīrtha, published as volume 106 in the Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series (Varanasi: Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series Office, 1998).
This is, of course, a reprint of the Nirnaya Sagar Press edition, which passed through several different printings, the most recent being in 1952.
This final section appears to contain miscellaneous items that did not fit easily or were overlooked during the preparation of the preceding sections, which are organized according to subject matter.

The citations throughout the *Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra* (SRB) are not provided with consistent precision, a fact which is reflected in this edition; nevertheless, we have attempted to place the references adjacent to each verse for the reader’s convenience. However, inconsistencies remain in the numbering due to discrepancies between the editions consulted by the original editor and those used by myself.
The following are some of the abbreviations employed herein:
*Kā.nī.* = *Kāmandakīnītiḥ*. (Triv. Skt. Ser. no. xiv).
*kathā* = *Kathāsaritsāgara* of Somadeva.
*ku.saṃ.* = *Kumārasambhava*.
Cāṇī.sā. = Cāṇakyanītisāra;
nī.śa. = Nītiśataka;
pañca. = Pañcatantra.
pa.pu. = Padmapurāṇa. pra. = Prasaṅgābharaṇam. (Grantharatnamālā IV, 1011).
bṛ.cā. = Bṛhat Cāṇakyanīti. (This is available on the GGM as Cāṇakyanītidarpaṇa).

*bhartṛ.* = *Bhartṛhariśatakatrayam* (ed. Bohlen). There is some confusion regarding verses attributed to Bhartṛhari; I have attempted to identify them according to their respective *śataka*, though I have not always been successful.
*bhartṛ.saṃ.* = *Bhartṛharisubhāṣitasaṅgraha* (ed. D.D. Kosambi).
*bhā.pu.* = *Bhāgavatapurāṇa*.
Bhoja = *Bhojaprabandha*. Ma.bhā. = *Mahābhārata*. Manu = *Manusmṛti*.
rā. = Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; rā.ta. = Rājataraṅgiṇī;
vikrama. = Vikramacaritam
Ve. = *Vetālapañcaviṃśati* vai.śa. = *Vairāgyaśataka* śā. = *Abhijñānaśakuntalā* (Kālidāsa)
Śā.pa. = Śārṅgadhārapaddhati;
Śṛ.ti. = Śṛṅgāratilaka;
Śṛ.śa. = Śṛṅgāraśataka.
saṃ.pā. = *Saṃskṛtapāṭhopakārakatattvabodhinī*. su. = *Subhāṣitāvali* of Vallabhadeva. hi. = *Hitopadeśa*.

In accordance with GGM’s policy of prioritizing quantity over quality, this text has not been sufficiently proofread or collated against its original sources. Nevertheless, I believe it is a useful addition for those interested in *subhāṣita*—witty, epigrammatic, instructive, and descriptive verses.
The seventh chapter, the Miscellaneous Section:
"Virtue is the primary quality in a person; he in whom that virtue perishes in this world..."
He has no need for life, nor for wealth, nor for kinsmen.
(1) [Mahābhārata 5.34.46] For even a base person, having attained the destruction of a great foe, attains praise;
just as the honey-gatherer, though struck by the elephant’s ear, [is praised for his persistence]. (2) [Bhāgavata 31]
For one who vies with the great, calamity alone is more grievous;
for the breaking of tusks is indeed praiseworthy for elephants when splitting mountains. (Pañcatantra 1.404) A jackal, with a great deal of beef, attempts to overcome a five-faced lion.
He who was nourished by me every day with curd-rice and milk-porridge—
(4) if even one of the five senses of a mortal man has a flaw, then his wisdom leaks away like water from a cracked jar. (5) [Mahābhārata 5.2047]
By honoring only these five in this world, one attains pure renown:
the gods, the ancestors, human beings, mendicants, and guests as the fifth.
Whatever cause there may be for sorrow, fear, or even suffering—
Or rather, one should abandon even that single limb from which effort originates.
[Śānti-parvan 1461] Those whose waters are silent and yet who roar most terribly in a region harsh with thick stones;
those who are clear at the proper time but become corrupted by turbidity when the clouds are darkened.
Even rivers that descend from noble lineages are seen to flow according to the direction, place, and time;
this is true: even for the great, these two (direction and time) cause them to engage in conduct consistent with their own nature.
Yama, the son of Vivasvat, makes one repay for their evil deeds.
"The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the witness of one's actions, dwells in the heart; he is pleased with him [who acts rightly].
[MBh 1.3018] "One should act with caution as long as danger has not arrived;
but having seen that danger has arrived, one should strike fearlessly. [MBh 1.5622]
Those who consume air are declared to be the multitude of reptiles; those known as "possessing coils" are the elephants that ward off singing bees with their broad ears;
and that tree which undergoes transformation through the internal heat it contains is called the *śamī*.
By thus prattling without restraint, "by the world," everything has been subverted.

(Rā.Ta. 3.194) A woman devoted to her husband, for whom her husband is her very life, and who delights in her husband’s pleasure and welfare—he who possesses such a wife is a blessed man on this earth. (Pañca. 3.144)

The Dharma is told in brief; O people, what is the use of elaboration? Helping others leads to merit, while harming others leads to sin. [13] A radiant young woman, full of grace and resplendent with a white parasol—
Prosperity is experienced as if stable while auspicious deeds flourish;

yet when those deeds are utterly severed, like a pearl necklace whose string has snapped in the play of love’s quarrel, it suddenly falls away from sight, scattering in all directions. (Bhartṛhari 1.95)
A bow that is both flexible and straight, a friend who does not falter in times of distress, and a wife born of a pure lineage— these are difficult to find.
(Pañcatantra 2.188) Just as an impression made upon a new vessel does not change otherwise, so too is this true for those things well-established.
Under the guise of a story, the ethics for children are here set forth:
(16) Even that which one knows to be exalted, one should proclaim in a lowly manner;
endowed with humility, one should describe its excellence through action. (17)
Kings speak but once; the virtuous speak but once;
daughters are given away but once—these three things happen only once and once. (18) [Ve.
34] The face is serene and the gaze is pure.
A passion for conversation, sweet speech, excessive affection, and a look of agitation are the signs of a person who is constantly devoted. (19) [Hi. 2.59]

Five will follow you wherever you go: friends, enemies, neutrals, those who depend on you, and those upon whom you depend. He who, without considering the relative strength and weakness of himself and his enemies, [proceeds... [Mahābhārata 5.1046]
Out of delusion, he rises up for the sake of action; he thus courts calamities.
One who desires prosperity should not, even in thought, desire conflict with one more powerful than himself when his own strength is inferior.
For one who is utterly weak is not slain, since the destruction of the state of a moth is evident. Even a man endowed with strength, if he possesses intelligence... [Pañca. 3.126]... [is not slain].
One should lead another toward enmity, but not do so oneself; for what wise person would consume poison without cause, thinking, "I have a physician"? (Pañcatantra 3.111)
On the touchstone of adversity, a man learns the true worth of friends, kinsmen, and relatives, as well as his own intellect and fortitude.
Indeed, it is friends alone who protect; one who possesses friends does not perish.

Even enmity born from a friend cuts away the very roots [of one's welfare]. (25) [Rāmāyaṇa 4.20.18] For the sake of a friend and for the sake of a kinsman, the wise man always exerts himself; when calamities have arisen, Manu spoke these words with effort: (26) [Pañcatantra 1.346]
The wind proclaims the proximity of the rutting elephant by the scent of his ichor;
and the lightning, manifesting its brilliance, clearly declares the thundering onset of the cloud—
both of which reveal their true nature only through the skill of the wise.
The grace of the Lord bestows prosperity upon those who are unaware of it, even upon a creature whose mental disposition remains steadfast from acquaintance in previous births.
The blackness of the *kālakūṭa* poison does not depart merely through contact with Śiva.
People do not desire one whose favor is fruitless and whose anger is also useless;
they do not wish him for a lord, just as women do not wish a eunuch for a husband.
[Bhoja-prabandha 57] One who increases his progeny, increases righteousness, and is his own kinsman...

He who, having honored and propitiated one who is advanced in knowledge as well as advanced in age, consults them regarding what should and should not be done, shall never be deluded. (Mahābhārata 5.155)
Just as a certain man traveling to another village might stay somewhere for a while, and having abandoned that dwelling, would set out again on the following day. (31)
In the same way, O descendant of Kakutstha, for human beings, father, mother, home, and wealth are merely a place of residence; the wise do not become attached to them.
Just as shadow and sunlight are always closely bound to one another, so too are these things linked to the body.
In this way, action and the agent are mutually connected.
(Pañcatantra 2.136) Just as ripe fruits have no fear other than falling, so for a man who is born, there is no fear other than death. (Pañcatantra 2.137)
Just as a field sown without seed becomes fruitless,
so too destiny does not succeed without human effort.
(35) [MBh 13.301] He who represents himself to virtuous people as being one way when he is actually otherwise—

He is the greatest evildoer in the world, for by that [neglect] he robs his own self. (Manu 4.255) Even one who is slightly immersed in the waters of the ocean of nectar— which is tranquil, possessed of infinite majesty, pure conscious bliss, and free from the succession of waves— does not drink.
Exhausted and deluded, one drinks from, sips, wades into, delights in, sinks into, and then emerges from the water of a mirage-ocean that is utterly devoid of substance—
when father, son, or friend has fallen under the power of death. (37)
Fools of dull intellect torment themselves excessively with grief, beating their bellies;
but for the wise, in this essence-less saṃsāra whose final outcome is bitter, separation only strengthens detachment by spreading the bliss of tranquility. (38) [Pr. 95]
For destiny alone remains awake to accomplish the welfare of those destined for it,
even as they remain unconscious of it, just as good servants serve their masters.
Playing at will, they destroy lineages, just as great rivers wash away entire families.
Prajāpati quickly declared all these faults with his mind:

"Rāma did not recognize the golden deer; Nahuṣa yoked the twice-born brahmins to his chariot; and the thought of stealing a cow with her calf arose in Arjuna only because he was a brahmin. (Mahābhārata 13.1475)
At the game of dice, the son of Dharma gave away his own four brothers and his queen;

for generally, even a virtuous man is abandoned by his intellect at the time of destruction. (41) [Verse 15] Formerly, learning existed for the destruction of the afflictions of those with stainless minds.
In the past, she descended into the realm of sensual pleasures for the sake of those seekers of sense-objects;
but now, beholding the rulers of this small fragment of earth who have turned their backs on the scriptures—alas, what misery!—she herself sinks lower and lower day by day. (Bhartṛhari 3.100)
A king without dharma, a twice-born man without purity, a yogi without knowledge,
a beloved without truth, a horse without speed, light without an ornament,
a warrior without valor, austerity without a vow, and a singer without melody— [are all useless].
Just as men abandon a brother without affection, the wise quickly forsake one who is devoid of Hari.
Even the entreaties of beloved women, though accompanied by sweet words, are rendered tasteless without the essence of love. [Saptaratna 2]
It does not enter the hearts of those who know it,
like a gem set with artificial color.
Whether it be pride, arrogance, specialized knowledge, delusion, or keen intellect—
Everything perishes at once when a man is destitute of wealth. ||45||
One who is thoroughly disciplined attains the state of being worthy of service by kings; discipline is their ornament—
like an elephant in rut whose trunk moves gently as it bestows gifts.
Like a noble elephant, he shines through his discipline.
[Kāvyālaṅkāra 1.65] He who pleases his father with virtuous conduct is a son;
that which seeks only the welfare of its husband is a wife.
That friend who acts with equanimity in both adversity and prosperity—these three things in this world are obtained by those who have performed meritorious deeds. [Bhartṛsaṃ.
279] A son begotten upon one’s wife is like one’s own face reflected in mirrors.
The progenitor rejoices upon seeing him, like a doer of merit who has attained heaven.
He who harms even harmful beings is merciless; he goes to a terrible hell, how much more so one who harms those that are auspicious? (Pañcatantra 3.16)
But whatever association with the virtuous there may be in saṃsāra, being intent on the taste of pleasure, that is placed at the forefront of sufferings because it ends in separation. (50) [Hi.
4.77] Whether it be a venerable kinsman, a beloved son, a brother, or even a friend—
One who, out of delusion, turns away from blameless action should be abandoned by one seeking what ought to be done.
For is this not a well-known saying in the world, which even women sing:
"What is the use of that gold which serves only for the cutting off of one's ear? (Pañcatantra 1.240)
The abode white as nectar, the moon with its shimmering spotless rays,
the lotus-face of a beloved, the exceedingly fragrant sandalwood powder,
and the garlands with their heart-pleasing scent— all these belong to the person who possesses passion.
It causes internal agitation, but not in one who is averse to contact with sense objects. //52//

Those who have wives perform sacred rites; those with wives are householders. Those who have wives rejoice; those who have wives are endowed with prosperity. (53) [Mahābhārata 1.3029] Regarding mantras, holy places, brahmins, gods, astrologers, medicine, and teachers—
Whatever one’s meditation is, such is the accomplishment that follows.
[Vikrama 64] Her two arms are lotus stalks, her lotus-face is the water of the play of beauty, her hips are the bathing-stone, her eyes are minnows, and the braided hair upon her head is the moss.
The Creator fashioned this beautiful lake for those burnt by the fires of Kāma’s arrows to bathe therein— the pair of cakravāka birds that are the breasts of the beloved.
(Śṛṅgāratilaka 1.55) A wife, a son, and a slave— these three alone are traditionally held to be without property.
Whatever they acquire for you belongs to him from whom it was received.

(Manu 8.416) A wise man should approach the king through those who are dear and beneficial to him, whose words are especially worthy of being heeded; he should not do so otherwise. (Pañcatantra 1.32?)
The forest of existence is terrifying; this body is a house full of many cracks.
Time is a powerful thief, and the night of delusion is perpetually dark.
Taking up the sword of knowledge, the shield of renunciation, and the armor of ethical discipline—
O people, having attained composure, remain awake with a most steady gaze.
It is not the way of the wise to reject happiness that has arrived, nor to place hope in future happiness. (MBh 12.5280)
First, the wife established in virtue awaits her husband after death;
having died first, she follows her deceased husband hereafter.
First, no knowledge was acquired; secondly, no wealth was earned. (Mahābhārata 1.3033)
"No merit was earned in the third; what will be done in the fourth? [Cā.nī.sā.
93] This one has lips red as a bimba fruit, a pair of jar-like breasts with the pride of burgeoning youth, a deep navel, a naturally curved hairline, and a waist that is quite slender.
"Let these things indeed forcibly and quickly produce what the mind has conceived here; yet that my cheeks—which are so clear—should repeatedly burn with perspiration is not fitting. (Pañcā.
1.221) He who delights in objects of various splendors, even in the worthless rainbow of Indra...

"Seeing my plumage here, what dear thing would he not do out of love? Thus thinking, that peacock dances upon the water-drops, displaying his rows of feathers; who else besides this cloud could be so void of heart as to abandon him? (63) [Rā.Ta. 3.218]
The body alone is the abode of pleasure, and the body is also the abode of pain.
Whatever action the embodied being performs with the body, by that very means he experiences its result. (64) [Mbh.
12.5478] Without discipline, what is prosperity? What is night without the moon?
What kind of skill in speech can there be for one who is devoid of true poetry?
(65) The moonlight departs along with the moon; the lightning dissolves together with the cloud.
That women follow the path of their husbands is a truth understood even by the insentient. (66) [Kuṣāṇḍakāvya 4.33]
It is better for one to observe silence than to speak a falsehood; it is better for men to be impotent than to approach another's wife;
it is better to give up one's life than to take pleasure in the words of a slanderer.
Better is the eating of alms than the pleasure of tasting the wealth of others. [Hi.
1.137] In front, on the bank of the Revā, stands a mountain with exceedingly high peaks;
behind it, the excellent Śabara chief pursues him fiercely with arrows from his bow.
To the left is a lake, and to the right is the torment of a forest fire;
thus does the young fawn lament, unable either to go or to stay. (Nītiratna 5) The innate charms of playful women—
These very things flash forth in the heart of the deluded man; for passion is indeed innate to the lotus, and the six-legged bee surely wanders there in search of nectar.
The intellect of men declines through association with the base; it reaches a middling state through middling associates, and attains excellence through the best. (70) [Mbh.
3.30] For those great souls whose vast undertakings are to be accomplished and who are favored by the benedictions of affectionate friends...
For those whose undertakings rise through both policy and daring, who ascend to the heights of their desires, and who are devoted to pride,
exaltation, and valor— how can there be peace for them as long as their hearts, filled with indignation, have not reached the further shore of their objectives? (Pañcatantra 3.253)
O King, does the world not carry fuel upon its head in order to burn it?
Even while washing the roots of trees, the force of a river cuts them away.
Just as one is seen bound by the nooses of Varuṇa, so too is he perceived.
In this way, one should restrain evil; for this is the vow of Varuṇa.
(73) [Rāmāyaṇa 2.122.12] A mark of lac on the forehead, the impression of armlets around the neck, the blackness of collyrium upon the cheeks, and the emergence of the red dye of betel upon the eyes—
Seeing this ornament that provokes anger, the soft-eyed woman’s sighs came to an end for a long time within the heart of her lover’s play-lotus at dawn. (Amaru.
60) Shame, affection, sweetness of voice, intellects, and the splendor of youth—
The company of beloved women, sacrifice, equanimity, the destruction of suffering, and diversion;
righteousness, scripture, the wisdom of the preceptor of the gods, purity, and concern for conduct—all these come to living beings when the vessel of the belly is full. (Pañcatantra 5.91)
In a holy village or a great forest, taking up his begging bowl covered with a white cloth,

he enters door after door, afflicted by hunger, seeking to fill the cavern of his belly with food that is righteous in its acquisition and whose vicinity is smoky from the smoke of the fire-offerings made by the twice-born.
A proud living being has a protector, and is not again made wretched day by day among his equals.
[Bhartṛhari 3.24] That which is improper in place and time, detrimental to the future, unpleasant, and causes one's own humiliation;
Even though I have reflected upon it repeatedly with my intellect, I do not understand those words; for they are indeed the deadly poison *hālāhala*.
Having taken up objects never seen before, one remains unsuspecting.
Nights pass away for men, taking with them both the desired and the undesired.
[Mahābhārata 12.12519] A tree planted in a good field, its basin filled by pleasant words,
and its irrigation performed with the faultless water of mental clarity;

O King, that very thing which the giver desires indeed becomes the fruit in due time; thus, even though it may be fleeting, this tree of generosity triumphs over even the wish-fulfilling trees and the like.
Now, those who know this do not grieve here, whether [the gift] be permanent or impermanent.

"The nature of those who grieve cannot be altered otherwise. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.2.49) "Having attained excessive elevation, a man perishes without doubt, just like a silkworm; thus spoke King Uśanas. (Saṃvarta Smṛti 57)

O Goddess Thirst, if you are pleased with those whose minds are bound by the thread of hope for fields, villages, forests, mountains, towns, cities, islands, and the circle of the earth, and who contemplate what they have already acquired— if you cause their limbs to swell with pride; [then...]
Therefore, O friend, how could there be talk of peace for living beings even in hundreds of thousands of cosmic eggs? (82) [Pra.
35] Even a virtuous deed, however small it may be, when planted by those of merit among the ranks of the most exalted, surely becomes a tree with a hundred branches. (83) [Rā.Ta. 3.304]

Through excessive pride and great audacity, Fortune becomes a source of doubt even for great sovereigns who are intent on reckless deeds. (84) [Rājataraṅgiṇī 4.517] One whose body is limited in size is unable to measure the three worlds.

Tell me, how can a living soul perceive objects within the interior of the body without the union [of the senses]? For even a lamp with a fine flame placed inside a jar is unable to illuminate things within the house.
A wise man intent on showing no disrespect, striving for stable prosperity,
should leave no remnant of fire, no remnant of debt, and no remnant of an enemy.
[86] Excessive drinking of water and sitting on hard seats...

The depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus) and the suppression of natural urges— through daytime sleep and nighttime wakefulness— these six causes dwell as diseases within men. [Vikramorvaśīya 2.37]
Even enemies, when supported by the world, attain prosperity; yet once prosperous, they lead to destruction. Therefore, one should not cause the subjects to tremble.
[In this world,] even for the binding of quicksilver, which is exceedingly fickle—
Granted, no method at all is known for the mind of a woman. [Kathā 37.232] Giving what she does not desire, destroying what was done before,
showing disrespect, and recounting her misdeeds—
Forgetting one's name through the course of conversation is the characteristic of a person who has become dispassionate. (90) [Hi.
1.114] Between a wicked person and a serpent, a serpent is better than a wicked person.
A serpent bites only at the appointed time, but a wicked person strikes at every step.
One who is exceedingly endowed with virtue and possessed of discipline never overlooks even the slightest injury to living beings.
"Past and future entities, as well as those that exist at present—
having realized that these are fashioned by Time, you ought not to abandon your composure.
[MBh 1.244] "A wealthy man, possessed by anger and greed, loses his sense of reason."
Looking askance, with a parched mouth, a sinner, and a frowning face—[Hārīta 1.123].
One should endure harsh words and never harbor pride in any way.
When provoked to anger, one should speak kindly; when reviled, one should speak words of welfare. [Manu 6.47]
That wealth which is acquired through excessive hardship, that pleasure which comes from excessive greed,

and that livelihood which involves the oppression of others— these are never found among the virtuous. (96) [Mahābhārata 5.1521] Furthermore, one who bites his lower lip in anger and speaks harsh words [is not a true ascetic].
Who would wish to examine him, if he wishes to give away the earth?
Those who merely memorize the texts are superior to the ignorant; those who retain them in memory are better than those who merely memorize;
those who possess true knowledge are superior to those who merely retain them; and those who apply themselves with resolve are superior to those who possess knowledge. (Manu 12.103)
Whether through ignorance or knowledge, having performed a censurable action,
one who seeks liberation from it should not perform it a second time. (Manu 11.232) Do not harbor pride regarding wealth, kin, or youth.
Time carries away everything in the blink of an eye;
having understood this entire world to be composed of illusion, quickly abandon it and enter the state of Brahman. (Mohamudgara 100)

Like the dust raised by a goat’s hooves or by a broom, a person without wealth is shunned by people; like the shadow cast by a lamp or a bed, he is abandoned. (Pañcatantra 2.108) Just as flowers and fruits, even when not being urged, [fall of their own accord...]

Just as they do not transcend their own time, so too does previously performed karma [not fail its time]. (102) [Mbh. 12.6756] The sun does not enter into conjunction at the wrong time, nor does it go to the setting mountain at the wrong time.
Neither the moon nor the ocean garlanded with great waves waxes or wanes out of season.
He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin.
"For it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from sacrifice" (Manu 3.118).

"Having gained the trust of all people through the establishment of the sacred fires, through sacrifices, by wearing saffron robes, matted hair, and deerskins, one should then plunder them like a wolf" (Mahābhārata 1.5560).
Neither is one born nor does one die before the appointed time;
a child does not speak before the appointed time,
nor does one attain youth before the appointed time.

A sown seed does not sprout out of season. (MBh 12.26.11) But when a person is cast into the fire, his own performed karma follows him; therefore, a person should diligently accumulate merit little by little. (MBh 5.1550)
"The Agnihotra sacrifice, the three Vedas, the triple staff, and smearing oneself with ashes—these, Bṛhaspati says, are merely the livelihood for those devoid of wisdom and manly effort. (108) [Pra.
30] Neither birds nor serpents are intoxicated out of season.
In this world, neither deer nor elephants, nor even mountain-dwelling beasts, conceive offspring out of season; nor do the cold, heat, and rains arrive at the wrong time. (MaBh 12.26.10)
In this very way, those born of noble lineage, possessing a splendor like that of fire,
though patient and unassuming, lie hidden like fire within wood.
Indeed, it is only when that very fire is kindled by friction from the wood that it blazes forth.
That fire quickly consumes both the wood and the forest with its brilliance, as it were, with another's splendor.

(MBh 5.37.57) One should not be abusive, nor contemptuous of others, nor a betrayer of friends, nor a servant of the base; one should not be arrogant, nor follow a degraded course of conduct, but should avoid harsh and biting speech. (MBh 5.36.6)
Fire is a great brilliance in the world; it remains hidden within pieces of wood, yet it does not consume that wood as long as it is not ignited by others.
Just as a heap of cotton is instantly destroyed upon reaching fire, so too is the body consumed.

In the same way, all evil is destroyed by the current of the Gaṅgā. (114) [Vikramacarita 183] Even when striving, physicians cannot remove the pain of those who are being tormented by diseases and are spending vast amounts of wealth. (115) [Mahābhārata 12.318.30]
Seed sown in a non-field perishes right there within;
even a field without seed becomes merely a barren plot of ground.
(Manu 10.71) Intolerance, the abandonment of modesty, the loss of prosperity, and the decay of dharma—these arise from it.
Everything that resembles covetousness proceeds from greed. [Mbh.
12.5881] Even while still a mere calf, a scent-elephant subdues other elephants;
the venom of a young serpent is far more intense than its speed.
Even while in his childhood state, the Lord of the Earth is fully capable of protecting [the world];

indeed, this group is able to accomplish its own tasks by its very nature, not merely by age. (Vikramorvaśīya 5.18) He who, though unable, proceeds with an action out of a sense of honor, [is truly steadfast].
For he indeed becomes an object of ridicule and faces a threat to his very life. (119) [Saṃ.
39] One should conquer the angry with non-anger; one should conquer the wicked with goodness;
one should conquer the contemptuous with generosity; and one should conquer the untruthful with truth. (120) [Mbh. 5.1518]
A Brahmin who persists in acts leading to downfall, in improper occupations,
who is hypocritical and considers himself wise despite his evil deeds, becomes equal to a Śūdra.
(MBh 3.206.11) One who is free from anger is superior to those who are prone to anger.
Likewise, one who endures is superior to one who does not;
humans are superior to non-humans; and the wise man is superior to the ignorant, just as a chariot is superior to one who lacks it. (Mahābhārata 1.3556)

Death indeed drags one away even while tasks remain unaccomplished; therefore, one should be devoted to righteousness while still young, for life is without certainty. As for that Śūdra who is ever intent upon self-restraint, truth, and dharma—
I consider him to be a brahmin; for by one's conduct alone does one become twice-born.
(MBh 3.206.12) Humility destroys ill-repute; prowess destroys misfortune;
forbearance constantly destroys anger; and right conduct destroys inauspiciousness. (MBh 5.1488)
For one who possesses nothing, who is pure, and who has attained [liberation] in every respect,
I perceive no equal when surveying the three worlds. (126) [MBh 12.6570] The virtuous, who are devoted to the rise of good conduct, experience the constraints that arise [from their practice].

Everywhere, those who live in constant fear of public scandal endure perpetual suffering; yet the common person is fortunate, for one of unrefined intellect is neither distressed by what is done well nor by what is ill-done, his heart being devoid of the discrimination between what is appropriate and what is inappropriate. (Daśarūpaka 3.18)
Wandering about as one who possesses nothing, you will experience happiness;
indeed, one who possesses nothing sleeps happily and likewise rises with ease.
An undertaking begun at an improper time is not conducive to achieving its purpose.
That very same thing, when undertaken at the proper time, conduces to great purpose.
[Mahābhārata 12.5006] Yesterday, we saw it with its smile-like white lotus-bud form, its beard awakening to life;
today, by its impetuousness, it has taken on the luster of molten copper.
In the morning, our face— withered by old age, with its strength and hair decayed, resembling the head of an aged goat— will surely be mocked by long-enduring spirits.
[130] It is unable to endure adversity, exceedingly deficient, and possesses a foolish and addicted leader.
A fortress that is unguarded and defended by cowardly warriors is said to be in a state of calamity.
(131) Whose body is truly secure, when even after performing improper acts and accumulating sin, one is still provided with what is beneficial? (132)
This slope of breasts is lofty,
the waist is sunken, and the hips are elevated;
how uneven is the body of this fawn-eyed maiden!
Who indeed does not stumble upon a new body? ||133||
One should not drink that intoxicant by which one fears the performance of improper acts, the avoidance of duties, or the disclosure of secrets at an inappropriate time. (134)
He who desires those who do not desire him, and abandons those who do desire him, and he who hates one who is powerful—him they call a person of deluded mind. (135)
"O beloved, regarding the waist between your breasts and your hips,
the doubt as to whether it exists or not does not cease for me even now. (Kāvyālaṅkāra 2.217) "The body of one who desires a woman who does not desire him is consumed by fever."
For one who desires her when she desires him, his pleasure becomes beautiful. ||137||
No action whatsoever is ever seen here in this world that is performed by one who is free from desire;
for whatever anyone does, all that is the movement of desire. (138)
The first refuge is one’s own self; the second refuge is one’s offspring;
the virtuous are said to be the third refuge; and the fourth is the accumulation of merit. (139) [Rā.
2.62] For people, there is no sudden advancement, nor is there a sudden decline.
And due to the lightness of their intellect, they are unable to properly distinguish between what is auspicious and inauspicious, nor to exercise greatness of mind. ||140||

One should not allow these to dwell in one's house: one who is habitually inactive, one who eats excessively, one who is hated by the world, one who is full of deceit, one who is cruel, one who lacks knowledge of place and time, and one who has an unpleasing appearance. (141)
O Bhārata, those who are attached to purposes and not to specific details—I consider them to be wise, for specific details lead to entanglement.
Do this very day what is beneficial; being old, what will you do?
For even one's own limbs become a burden when things have gone awry.
The lower lip has the hue of a young sprout, the arms resemble tender branches, and youth, as alluring as a flower, has taken its place upon her limbs. (144)
The best of men say there are four vices for rulers of the earth: hunting, drinking, gambling, and excessive attachment to sensual pleasures. (145)
He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—one of these two perishes or incurs enmity. ||146||
He who does not acquire the eternal Dharma by means of this unstable body that perishes at every moment is a person of deluded mind and is to be pitied. (147)
This delight in dwelling in a village is the tethering rope;
having severed it, the virtuous depart, but the wicked do not sever it.
(148) [Mahābhārata 12.169.24] For embodied beings, old age is the path; for mountains, water is old age.
Non-enjoyment of women is old age; the arrow of harsh words is the old age of the mind. 149.
Previously, when my desire was not yet attained, the three watches of the night seemed to pass as if multiplied a hundredfold;
but if it were even so at the time of union with you, [it would be different].
O fair-browed one, as that [feeling] spreads forth, I shall then become successful. ||150||
Becoming mild, gentle, and emaciated, the enemy slowly withdraws;

like an anthill around a tree, he later cuts away its roots. (151) [Hv 1168] Those who are unaccustomed to the path find their gait sluggish in poetry, and they are weary in the thickets of the sciences.

Those who are ignorant of suffering, mute regarding the transformations of speech, indifferent to the virtues of others, and who have never attended the assemblies of the wise— how indeed could they serve as touchstones for the itching of others' eloquence? (152)
Through the lack of practice in the sciences, through lack of association with the wise, and through the failure to restrain the senses, calamity arises for men. (153)

A wise person, having rescued with all their power a neutral friend who has fallen into calamity through folly, should then reprove them for their own benefit. [Kavitā 76] [One should avoid] useless exile from one's home.
He who does not cultivate alliances with the wicked, does not violate the wives of others, and does not indulge in wretchedness, theft, slander, or the drinking of intoxicants, is always happy. (155)
Seeing what is harmful as beneficial, and what is beneficial as harmful, the fool who is driven by his senses considers great suffering to be happiness. (156)
Abandoning kin, abandoning the body, and abandoning one's country—among these three, the first and the last involve prolonged suffering, while the middle is but a momentary fever. (157)
That which is unattainable through grief causes the body to suffer, and one's enemies rejoice; therefore, do not set your mind on sorrow.
Even through a successful union of two who are free from illness and longing, there is no pleasure for me; rather,
it is better for two who have lost all hope of attaining one another.
Even the destruction of the body is the same for those who are equal in passion. ||159||
One should destroy mental suffering with wisdom and physical suffering with medicines;
for this is the power of knowledge, which the foolish do not attain. (MBh 3.14079) One who lacks self-control and hates right conduct increases the prosperity of his enemies.
Even after attaining great sovereignty, one perishes along with it.
A king, even when impoverished, should not take what ought not to be taken;
nor, even when prosperous, should he relinquish what ought to be taken, however small the matter may be. 162.
One who, being himself at fault, provokes blameless people within his own circle does not sleep peacefully at night, like one living in a house with a snake (MBh 5.38.37). Furthermore,
by taking what should not be taken and by rejecting what should be taken...
The king's weakness is proclaimed; he perishes both in this world and after death. ||164||
That craving of human beings, which is without beginning or end and resides within the body, destroys them once it has arisen, like a fire not born from a womb. ||165||
An enemy must not be disregarded, even if he is weak, by one who is stronger;

for even a small fire burns, and even a tiny amount of poison kills. (166) [Mahābhārata 12.58.17] The Vedas have non-recitation as their impurity; for a Brāhmaṇa, the lack of observance of vows is his impurity.
The Vāhīkas are the impurity of the earth; falsehood is the impurity of a man. 167.
Some objects, such as the Tathāgatas, exist eternally without being produced;
even human effort would be rendered useless with respect to them. (168)
Indeed, for one who has committed acts such as hatred, another person appears falsely as something different and even more vivid than their own clear nature;
just as by one's own nature, one perceives the moon and other objects doubled before oneself.
For the eye, though consisting of light, is indeed afflicted by the defect of darkness.
Misfortunes quickly come upon one who behaves ignobly, lacks wisdom, is envious, and is unrighteous, as well as one who is foul-mouthed and prone to anger.
That the wind-bird remains within the cage of the nine unobstructed gates is itself a marvel; what need is there to speak of its departure from it? (171)
He who, devoid of intelligence, considers as truth merely what is spoken by others,

is an object of ridicule for others, like a shaven-headed ascetic perched upon a tree branch. (172) [Vṛttisaṃgraha 4.49] In this cyclic existence, where movement is like that of a wheel, dwelling with loved ones is impermanent.
This meeting on the road is indeed like that of a brother, a mother, a father, or a friend.
Ineffable, indivisible, limitless, and immutable, the love of the virtuous is like Brahman itself, cutting away the very root of suffering. (174)
Having done harm to one who is powerful, one should not feel secure thinking, "I am far away";
for these [enemies] fall upon the negligent like the movements of hawks. 175.
Perseverance is the root of prosperity; my beak is like iron;
days and nights are long—why does the ocean not dry up? (176)
Words that have come to contradict their own results are uttered by those who lack certainty, who fear decisive judgment, and who perceive hundreds of faults at every step.
They become objects of ridicule in the world. ||177||
He abandons his friend, leaves behind his circle of kinsmen, and swiftly departs from both his mother and his native land;
having become attached to the world of the undesired, he goes away to a foreign land.

A person whose mind is agitated by wealth does not hesitate; through union with the undesirable and separation from the beloved, men of little intelligence are joined with mental sufferings. (Pañcatantra 5.26) 178–179.
Free from envy, guarding his wife, sharing with others, speaking kindly, gentle, and sweet-spoken toward women, yet he should not fall under their control. (180)
Neither father, nor son, nor self, nor mother, nor circle of friends—here in this world and hereafter, the husband alone is always the refuge for women. (181)
Having carefully considered the consequences and the ripening of actions, as well as his own capacity, a wise person should either act or refrain from acting. (182)
One should examine the consequences in actions that entail consequences;
having deliberated thoroughly, one should act, and not proceed with impulsive haste.
And this worldly proverb appears true to me here:
"Men follow their fathers, while women follow their mothers. (184) Even if, by some stroke of fate, a woman does not follow her husband, she follows her mother.
Nevertheless, ethical discipline must be protected; through the breaking of ethical discipline, one falls downward. ||185||
But one who possesses many thoughts and mantras becomes detestable to practitioners;
because his mind is unstable, he is neglected by them in the performance of their tasks. (186)
O deluded one, abandon the thirst for the acquisition of wealth;
cultivate freedom from craving toward the body, intellect, and mind.
Whatever you obtain is acquired through your own past actions.
Dispel your mind with that wealth. [Mohamudgara 187] "O King, it is said that one who is inwardly corrupt yet outwardly patient brings about all manner of misfortune;
Śakuni and Śakaṭāra are the two examples in this regard. [188]

The ocean clearly transforms those countless water droplets that constantly roll within it into the state of precious pearls, embracing them with its onrushing circles of waves and taking them up once they have been seized by the clouds.
Generally, even one who is insignificant, if he has been shown respect by another, is honored by his masters upon arrival. ||189||

Where fools are not honored, where grain is well-stored, and where there is no quarrel between husband and wife—there Fortune has come of her own accord. (Bṛhac-Cāṇakya 3.21) The wise take delight in the extremes; they do not take delight in the middle states.
They say that the attainment of the final goal is happiness, while the interval between the two final states is suffering.
One should constantly cut off the root of the enemy's faction from the very beginning;
thereafter, one should eliminate their allies and all those belonging to that side.
Having eaten from these vessels containing the leftovers of others, the lords of the earth [attain their ends].
Why did they not feel shame, or why did they not maintain a concern for purity? ||193||
Another enjoys the wealth of one who has gone to the realm of the departed;
birds and fire consume the elements of the body;
and he departs for the next world accompanied by two things alone.
Enveloped by both merit and demerit.
Fickle by nature, difficult to serve, and likewise difficult to grasp in their true essence, the fortunes of this world are just like the words of a wise man. (195)
Through mutual support and by relying upon one another, kinsmen flourish together like lotuses in a lake. (196)
For another indeed does not eat the fruit of the action performed;
that very doer alone is the partaker of pleasure and pain,
whatever action has been performed by him.
One attains that; there is no destruction of what has been done. (MBh 3.13868) Without exertion, no task whatsoever is accomplished;
indeed, deer do not enter the mouth of a sleeping lion. (198)
That lowest of men who places his trust in one who has done him harm does not live long, just like one who is helpless and weak.
Out of greed alone, foolish men— even those endowed with wealth and learning— [act thus].
They are separated from what should not be done and are led astray even into difficult paths. [Hi.
1.34] For another does not eat the fruit of the action performed; rather, the doer himself is the one who experiences pleasure and pain.
Whatever action has indeed been performed by him, that he experiences; there is no destruction of what has been done.
Just as the sun shines within the sky, having dispelled the intense darkness.

Having thus destroyed his evil, he shines, sprinkled by the waters of the Gaṅgā. (202) [Vikramorvaśīya 181] Even the flow of the Gaṅgā’s waters, upon reaching the ocean, necessarily becomes of its same essence; therefore, a wise man should not take refuge in that which is of an impure nature. (203) [Kāmandakīyanītisāra 5.8]
For happiness indeed ends in suffering, and sometimes happiness arises from suffering;
therefore, one who desires eternal happiness should abandon both of these.
Even if one has fallen into weakness or is ruined, it is better than the sight of what is desired.

Generally, for living beings, the force of suffering becomes increasingly greater. [Pañcatantra 2.174] Even by means of gentleness, a wise person constantly destroys the enemy by contracting his body, just as a creeper destroys a great tree. [Harivaṃśa 1167]

Seeking happiness through the pacification of the fear of the enemy of the serpents, Śeṣa, however, instead abandoned his own ease; for, having made his body a couch while serving the enemy of the Asuras,
he thereby acquired the capacity to endure affliction in that very state.
The burden-bearing of the earth has been undertaken and placed upon him for an endless time.
(207) [Rājatarangiṇī 3.215] For one who has no son, there is no destination; neither heaven nor even that [liberation].
Therefore, having seen the face of a son, one may afterwards indeed become an ascetic. (208) [Vikramacarita 85]
"One who has not done it before must not perform an action censured in the world;
but for one who has done it before, abandoning it is a great merit—so says the Śruti.
That undecaying one causes the pleasures and pains of living beings to age away. [MaBh 12.283.5]
For the sun indeed sets and rises again and again.
(MBh 12.318.7) One should extract the essence from everywhere, even from the prattle of a madman or the crawling of a child, just as one extracts gold from stones. (MBh 5)

Lack of faith, failure to provide support, the seizing of one's rightful share, wasting time, and the absence of remedy—these are the causes of disenchantment. (212) For living beings, pleasure and pain, which arise from the causes of affliction, should be regarded as equal. [H. 3.90]

On the head, there may be heat from the hair, yet it requires both oil and cutting [to remove it]. (213) [Dṛṣṭānta-śataka 47] What would be gained by crushing even those who are unpleasant if they are unable to endure suffering?
It is fitting for one to desire victory over those who are capable of uprooting that very suffering. (214) [Rāja-taraṅgiṇī 3.283]

For that king who is the giver of fearlessness is always worthy of worship; indeed, his sacrificial session (sattra) always has the gift of fearlessness as its fee. (215) [Mahābhārata 12] For a person experiences pleasure and pain in alternation.
"For no one, O bull among men, attains infinite happiness" (Bṛhacchānti 4.13).
"The ocean and you are both deep and unswerving from your bounds;
yet he resembles collyrium in hue, while you possess the luster of gold" (Kāvyālaṅkāra 2.183).
But he who, having understood the intention of his master,
performs all tasks without weariness—
one who is a speaker of what is beneficial, devoted, and noble— [is a true servant].
For he who knows one's capacity is to be pitied like one's own self.

(MBh 5.1358) Laziness is pleasure that ends in suffering; diligence is suffering that results in happiness. Prosperity, fortune, modesty, fortitude, and success do not dwell in one who is lacking in skill. (MBh 12.27.30)
But he who, though instructed, does not respect the word; and he who, when being exhorted,
speaks in opposition— such a person is arrogant in his own wisdom.
Such a servant must be abandoned with all haste.
For those men who possess pride yet do not know their own true strength,
their endeavors appear like those of the blind— their end being only a fall.
One should enjoy happiness when it arrives and endure suffering when it arrives;
one should wait for the appointed time, just as a farmer waits for his crops.
(222) Pride destroys the prosperity of a man of little intelligence.
A maiden is defiled by pregnancy, and a twice-born man by living at home. ||223||
Insomnia visits one who is prosecuted by a powerful man, one whose means are meager, one whose wealth has been stolen, one who is lustful, and a thief. (224)
Friendliness is easy to practice in every way, but its maintenance is difficult;
for because of the impermanence of mental states, joy is shattered by even a slight cause.
Since a powerful aggressor does not desist without having achieved his objective, no other form of peace exists except through the offering of tribute. (226)
Seeking success, one should serve a master who is distinguished, steadfast, meritorious, renowned, and practiced by the virtuous—just as one would serve the praiseworthy Lord of the Vindhyas. (227)
Just as this very body is like a bubble on the water, so too are riches as flickering as a lamp in a gale; for whose sake are they?
Indeed, one might exert the greatest effort toward the body. (Kathāsaṃgraha 22.40)
By means of such strategies as clothing and other gifts, a lord of men should never release an enemy in his kingdom, even if that enemy speaks with compassion;
he should not feel pity in that situation, but should slay one who has previously done him harm. (229–230)
Having attained elevation from an enemy, one should not trust in the thought, "I am exalted.
For by attaining such elevation, one may perish like an insect in a cloak.
For just as Bharata colors his own body with various pigments,
creating diverse forms, so too does the Self produce bodies born of karma. An enemy must not be released, even if he speaks piteously at great length.
One should not show compassion toward him; one must simply slay the wrongdoer. ||233||
An enemy becomes a friend, and even a friend may become hostile; for, due to the conjunction of circumstances and the requirements of tasks, the course of affairs always follows that very path. (234)

For one who possesses intelligence, power, splendor, vigor, perseverance, and resolve— from where can there be fear of returning to worldly existence? (MaBh 5.37.37) Both immortality and death are established within the body.
Through delusion one meets with death; through truth one attains immortality. ||236||

Sorrow does not touch a man who is intelligent, whose wisdom is perfected, who is desirous of hearing, free from envy, self-controlled, and has conquered his senses. [MBh 12.168.32] Whether he be intelligent or foolish, brave or timid, dull-witted or wise—
Whether weak or strong, one shares in happiness according to one's portion.

(238) [Mahābhārata 12.168.22] Through the merits of their previous births, all men obtain sons who are intelligent, handsome, virtuous, long-lived, and proficient in learning. (239) [Prasaṅgāparihāra]
"O Bhārata, actions performed with the intellect are the best; those with the arms are middling;
those with the legs are inferior, as are those involving the carrying of burdens.
The quarters of space are his garment, the hollow of his hand is his bowl, and deer are his friends. [Mahābhārata 5.35.65]

When will this intense regimen— meditative concentration, sleep, reclining on the ground, roots for food— be fully accomplished as desired by my heart’s activity, for the sake of accumulating supreme contentment? (241)
Asceticism is the limit of austerity; liberation is the limit of all virtues;

generosity is the limit of the arts; poetry is the limit of the joy of birth; a fair-faced woman is the limit of beauty; death is the limit of fear; and supporting those who have sought refuge is the limit of the lineage of the righteous.

The limit of hunger is not its end; the limit of the ear is the narration of Hari. (242) [Prasaṅga 10] When indeed the time of destruction ordained by fate is perceived, then a man sets his mind upon contrary things. (243) [Rāmāyaṇa 3.62.20]

O Ketakī, though you dwell among serpents, though you are incomplete, though you are thorny, though you are crooked, though you are born of the mud, and though you are difficult to approach— by your fragrance alone, you are dear to all living beings.
Indeed, a single virtue destroys all faults. (Bṛhaccāṇakya 17.21) "I am dear to you, and you are dear to me"—this is mere rumor;
"you are my life-breath, and I am yours too"—alas, this is but idle chatter.
"May you be mine and may I be yours; that would be good for us both, O Rādhā, for the use of the second-person and first-person pronouns is not appropriate between the two of us. (245)
People who seek to accomplish their own business honor those who are standing;
for what man would ever salute another who has fallen, even as an enemy? (246)
Whether flying up into the sky, going down to the surface of the earth, or running across the entire world, that which has not been given does not come to one. (247)
He who resolves a calamity once it has arisen is truly wise, just as the merchant’s paramour was concealed from view by his wife. (248)
What wonder is there in this, that for those who desire the fruit of wealth from the seed of knowledge which has tranquility as its fruit, their undertaking becomes fruitless?
For all things have fixed domains and do not undergo transformation.
A rice seed is capable of producing rice, but it can never produce a barley sprout. ||249||
One should not eat delicious food alone, nor should one contemplate matters of profit alone;
one should not travel the road alone, nor should one stay awake alone among those who sleep. (250)
Even he who is alone, has abandoned his home, uses only his hands as a bowl, and is clothed only by the directions—see the wonder!—even he is tormented in this world by craving. (251)
O Śambhu, when shall I become solitary, free from desire, peaceful, using my hands as a bowl, clothed only by the directions, and capable of uprooting karma? (252)
These two do not shine by means of contrary action: the householder who does not undertake worldly affairs, and the mendicant who is occupied with business. (253)
He is made to eat, yet he is not well; he is kept awake, yet he does not wake up;
he says nothing of his own accord—even as a servant, he merely lives here. (254)
One who manages his expenditures by spending only a fourth part of his income, like a lamp with an undiminished supply of oil, beholds prosperity for a long time. (255)
One who knows the virtues and faults regarding the future, who makes swift decisions in the present, and who understands the remaining consequences of past actions, is not overcome by enemies. (256)
Whatever may be pleasant to the taste both for the future and for the present, that alone one should do; one should not practice what is hated by the world. (257)
This is the fruit of desire in the world: that two people possess a single mind; for when desire is formed with another's mind, their union is like that of two corpses. ||258||
From this [ocean], the gods obtained the nectar; from this, Indra obtained the horse Uccaiḥśravas endowed with excellent qualities;
and from this, Kṛṣṇa obtained Lakṣmī, the sole abode of wondrous valor—such and other ancient stories have been heard by everyone.
But by us, not even a drop of sweet water has been seen anywhere here in this ocean. (259)
For the great must always maintain fortitude even in hardship, even in pain, and even in extreme peril;
thus they cross over difficulties without difficulty.
Those who are exalted by fortitude and skillful in practice. ||260||
Both those who have renounced and those who seek wealth cry out, "Give! Give!
as long as there is something; they never look [at the giver] to see whether he has it or not. (261)
Some are true men who accomplish the welfare of others by abandoning their own self-interest;
those who strive for the sake of others without contradicting their own interest are merely ordinary people;
but those who destroy the welfare of others for their own benefit are human rākṣasas.
But as for those who pointlessly destroy the welfare of others—who among us does not know them? (262)
There is no fixed rule regarding the favor of the rain-bearing god; he manifests that which brings intense pleasure to a living being only to produce displeasure in an instant,
swiftly extinguishing the heat of the sky during the long days of summer.
Having manifested from the lord of the forest (the sacrificial tree), he emits flashes of lightning.
(Sūkti 105.2) The goddess Śrī was in the house of the ten-faced Rākṣasa, the daughter of Janaka; and the blessed Triple Veda was led down to the subterranean realm by the Dānavas.
The lord of the Daityas, under the pretext of Pātālaketu, abducted Madālasā, the daughter of the Gandharva; alas, the workings of Fate are treacherous and perverse! ||264||
What is impossible for the wise?
What is unattainable for those who maintain firm resolve?
What is impossible for those of pleasant speech?
What is unattainable for those who apply themselves with effort in this world? ||265||
This ketaki flower, world-renowned for its fragrance and golden hue,
caused a fickle bee to fall into the midst of its blossoms through the delusion that it was a lotus;
blinded by the pollen of the flower, his wings were torn away by the thorns.
O friend, the bee is unable to do either: to stay or to go.

(266) [Padmaśrī-sūtra 19] For the sake of cows, for the sake of Brahmins, for the sake of one's master, or for the sake of a woman, he who would give up his life for the sake of his place [or home] shall attain eternal worlds. (267)
Cows see by scent, the twice-born by the Veda; kings see by means of spies, and other people with their eyes. (268) [Vikr.
117] Generosity, in my view, is a virtue superior to a hundred other virtues.
If learning also adorns him, what more can I say?
And if he possesses what is called valor, then homage be to him! It is truly a marvel that these three qualities do not envy one another. (269)

"Men should abandon pleasure born from contact with sense objects because it is beset by suffering"— this is the deliberation of fools, O fool; it is like one who wishes to discard rice grains that are rich in well-formed kernels.
O friend, who that desires their own welfare would indeed [desire] things mixed with chaff and husks? ||270||
Its fortress is Trikūṭa, its moat the ocean, its warriors are the Rākṣasas, its wealth comes from the Giver of Riches (Kubera),
and its treatise on statecraft was composed by Uśanas.
That Rāvaṇa met his downfall through the power of fate. (Garuḍa Purāṇa 113) In all cases, the conduct of those whose virtues are beyond perception is to be inferred from their actions;
therefore, one should discern the deeds of those whose conduct is hidden by means of their results. (Hitopadeśa 4.106)
What is the use of an elephant in rut that performs no royal duties?
Whether he be large or small, a man who performs his duty is superior. (273)
What is the use of sandalwood with camphor, or what is the use of ice-cold things?
All of those are not worth even a sixteenth part of the body of a friend.
An old man is neither able to enjoy nor able to renounce the objects of the senses.
Like a dog with bared teeth, he merely licks with his tongue;
for this moon has not become her face through truth, nor has the pair of blue lotuses attained the state of her eyes, nor has her slender body been fashioned even from gold. (275) [Hi. 1.113]

But thus, with minds deceived by poets, foolish people serve the flesh-and-bone bodies of deer-eyed women, even though they know the true nature of reality. (Śṛṅgāraśataka 46) Heirs become arrogant toward one who has desisted from an undertaking out of fear of expenditure.
Servants will not do anything pleasing for a ruler whose mind is intent only on receiving recompense;

rather, when his accumulated wealth is being seized and his life is at stake, they would always exert themselves as if against an enemy. What unpleasant thing, then, would not be done out of greed? (277) [Rājataraṅgiṇī 5.190]
"I am a cuckoo and you are a crow; our blackness is equal.
